title: Mexico cuts to 6.25% as slack is expected to limit peso pass-through
summary: A three-member majority of Banxico’s Board cut the overnight target by 25 basis points to 6.25%, effective 6 November. Victoria Rodríguez Ceja, José Gabriel Cuadra García and Omar Mejía Castelazo supported the reduction. Galia Borja Gómez and Jonathan Heath preferred to hold at 6.50%. The majority described its move as an individual adjustment and judged that maintaining the new rate for a prolonged period would support convergence. The two elements have different pricing implications. A reduction at the current meeting and a signal to leave the new rate in place can shift the first few expected overnight settings without implying an extended sequence of cuts.

The Board’s central argument concerned exchange-rate transmission. The peso had depreciated since the preceding decision and higher depreciation featured among the upside risks. But the majority considered that persistent slack would limit how far currency movements reached consumer prices. The economy continued expanding in the third quarter, yet the Bank expected spare capacity to persist and saw downside risks to activity. It judged demand pressure absent and restraint from existing policy still at work. These claims explain why the observed sign of the currency move was insufficient to determine the policy vote. The release does not give an estimated pass-through coefficient, a currency threshold or a separate rationale for either dissenter.

Between the first halves of September and October, headline inflation rose from 3.42% to 3.62% because of non-core components. Core inflation edged down from 3.79% to 3.78%. Year-end inflation expectations fell and longer ones remained stable above target. Both the forecast revisions and the numerical guidance were modestly adverse in the near term. Q4 2026 headline inflation was revised from 3.5% to 3.7%, principally because non-core inflation had been stronger than expected. The Q4 core projection rose from 3.6% to 3.7%. The following four quarters remained at 3.4%, 3.3%, 3.2% and 3.0% for both headline and core. Thus the baseline converged to target in 2027 Q4 even after the higher estimate for the current quarter. The seasonally adjusted annualised quarter-on-quarter memorandum shows faster Q4 2026 headline momentum of 4.4%, a different measure from the annual forecast of 3.7%.

The Board still saw inflation risks tilted upwards. More persistent core inflation, greater peso weakness, trade disruption, geopolitical conflict, weather and costs could each delay convergence. Weaker activity in Mexico or the US and lower pass-through from costs would work in the opposite direction. US policy changes and an extended conflict could generate effects on either side. That distribution helps explain the guidance: a conditional cut and a pause can coexist with a central forecast that reaches 3% and considerable uncertainty around it.

Market evidence in the announcement was horizon-specific. Mexican short government yields had risen since the last meeting, while medium and long yields had fallen. US yields fell at most maturities over the interval even though longer rates reached multidecade highs within it. An intraperiod peak and the net change between endpoints can have opposite signs. Global financial markets remained volatile and the Fed had left its policy range unchanged in October. None of these observations is a measurement of the immediate response to Mexico’s cut. To distinguish a surprise about the current rate from news about how long it would stay there, a researcher needs a pre-announcement curve, the first liquid post-announcement prices and a check on concurrent global moves.

questions.question: Does weak demand actually reduce exchange-rate pass-through in the sectors most exposed to imports?
questions.detail: Compare producer and final consumer prices across import-intensive categories with differing sales and capacity conditions. Allow for exchange-rate lags, hedges and existing inventories. The Board’s rationale concerns the ability to pass costs through, so a rise in import costs without a similar consumer-price response would be more informative than a correlation between the aggregate peso and headline CPI.

questions.question: How did the market distinguish a single adjustment from a resumed cutting cycle?
questions.detail: Estimate the pre-meeting probability of 25 basis points, then compare immediate changes in short meeting rates and later forwards. The majority signalled an extended stay at the new level, and two members preferred no cut. Different movements along the curve could reveal whether the action or the accompanying duration guidance supplied the larger surprise.

questions.question: Can inflation reach 3% in late 2027 if the near-term core forecast rises again?
questions.detail: Compare quarterly forecast vintages with incoming service and goods prices, separating base effects from sequential momentum. Track whether the projected 3.4%–3.0% path in 2027 continues to hold or is revised when new observations enter. A succession of revisions migrating outward along the forecast horizon would pose a different risk from a one-quarter non-core surprise.
